justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish but essentially sideways drift from what I understood to be the prevailing gold price level around $1,760–$1,770 per troy ounce at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, adding only a slight upward nudge given gold's tendency to exhibit mean-reverting behavior over very short windows and the modest positive carry from safe-haven demand at the time. For the one-week estimate, I edged slightly higher to reflect the mild medium-term upward trend that had been present, while for the one-month estimate I projected a somewhat larger drift upward, consistent with the slow structural demand for gold as a hedge against inflation and dollar weakness, without assuming any dramatic catalyst.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by the scaling of uncertainty with time horizon, which is standard for financial assets following something close to a random walk. Over one day, realized volatility in gold tends to run roughly 0.6–0.9% annualized daily, which translates to a fairly tight band. Over one week, that uncertainty compounds, and over one month it widens considerably. I also factored in that gold is particularly sensitive to Federal Reserve communications and real interest rate movements, both of which can shift rapidly and unpredictably, adding fat tails to the distribution beyond what simple volatility scaling would suggest.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the upside, a significant escalation in geopolitical tensions — such as a broadening of conflict in Eastern Europe or the Middle East — could trigger a sharp safe-haven surge, potentially pushing gold $100 or more above my one-month upper bound. A sudden pivot or pause signal from the Federal Reserve could also compress real yields sharply and send gold meaningfully higher. On the downside, a surprisingly hawkish Fed meeting, a strong dollar rally, or a broad risk-on environment where investors rotate out of defensive assets could push prices toward or below the lower bound of even my one-month interval.

It is also worth noting that gold markets can be affected by large institutional positioning shifts, ETF flow dynamics, and central bank buying or selling programs that are not fully visible in public data. These structural flows can override short-term macro signals and introduce discontinuous jumps that probabilistic models based on historical volatility tend to underweight. My intervals are therefore best understood as capturing the central mass of likely outcomes under normal market functioning, rather than guaranteeing containment of all plausible scenarios.
